narrative:
High pressure stretches from here to off the New England Coast. We are now in a warmer flow, making the next three days exceedingly pleasant. A front passes through Thursday night, but you will not notice any difference. You will notice high clouds developing, though; they thicken Saturday as a tropical system strengthens in the Gulf of Mexico. Isaias will be the name. It comes ashore between Mobile and Biloxi late Friday night. It then rides up the Natchez Trace into West Tennessee and eventually into Indiana (late Sunday) before being swept ENE. We become caught in a conveyor of moisture, far from the center of the storm, Saturday night and Sunday. The east side of the Appalachians will see the most rain--4 to 6 inches with locally higher totals. You have time to prepare, and do.

The September 2026 Weather Recap is available. We set or tied lots of record high temperatures last month. The details on that story and lots more are in the Weather Recap.

Subscribe Forecast Discussion High pressure anchored off the New England coast holds the mountains in a warm southerly flow through Friday. Wednesday and Thursday are sunny and warm for October, and a dry front crossing Thursday night changes nothing but the wind. Friday stays warm with high clouds arriving from the southwest. Tropical Storm Isaias is the story of the weekend. It strengthens over the central Gulf and comes ashore on the Mississippi coast late Friday night. The high over New England blocks its path to the northeast, so the center jogs north through Mississippi and Tennessee toward Indiana, far to our west. Our rain does not come from the center. Between that New England high and Isaias, a strong southeast flow sets up off the Atlantic, and that conveyor of tropical moisture rides up the east face of the Blue Ridge from Saturday night through Sunday. High clouds thicken Saturday morning, rain develops during the afternoon, and the heaviest rain falls Saturday night into Sunday morning. Rain tapers to showers late Sunday as the center passes to our north. The east side of the Appalachians takes the most water. Stream and river flooding is a concern, but know this is NOT Helene! Monday brings scattered morning showers, in a northwest flow around the exiting system. Showers are mostly on the west side of the Appalachians, under lingering clouds; how quickly the moisture leaves Monday is uncertain at this time. A cold front crosses Tuesday with a few afternoon showers, then Wednesday clears with cooler air behind it. Detailed forecast discussion and analysis is only available to RaysWeather supporters. All Photos Submit Photo Latest Insights September 2026 Weather Recap Monthly Recap for the Southern Appalachians A heat dome aloft sat over the southern Plains and the South for most of the month. Air sinks under a heat dome. It warms, dries out, and shuts down rain. We sat on its eastern edge. The national temperature anomaly map below shows the hottest areas right under it. Three times, strong high pressure over New England sent shallow cool wedges down the east side of the Appalachians (September 6–7, 15, and 23–24). With the dome still overhead, these cool periods lasted only a day or two. The heat dome finally weakened after the 18th. An upper-level low moved from the Ohio Valley to the Mid-Atlantic, passing just north of us, and brought the month's wettest stretch (September 18–24). It then stalled off the coast as the Nor'easter. The Northeast got the storm. We got dry, cooler northwest breezes (September 26–28). Figure 1: September 2026 Temperature Anomaly, Contiguous U.S. (PRISM) The national precipitation map below tells the same story. Under the heat dome, much of the South received less than half its normal rain. Our region was less dry, averaging about 70 percent of normal at our stations. The exception was a narrow band along the Blue Ridge and in southwest Virginia, where southeasterly flow ahead of the September 18–24 upper low pushed Gulf and Atlantic moisture upslope. A few violent storms formed in that flow, and some areas got heavy rain on multiple days. A few spots there finished near or above normal. Figure 2: September 2026 Precipitation, Percent of Average, Contiguous U.S. (PRISM) The Big Story The big story for September was unseasonably warm weather. Despite the cool interludes, temperatures for the Southern Appalachians averaged 5 degrees above normal. The cover image shows the deviation of average temperatures from normal for September. The heat was most intense in the first five days of September, but record highs were also set or tied later in the month. Temperatures were 10–15 degrees above average for almost a third of the month. The table below lists every record high set or tied that we found in the region, counting only stations with enough climate history for the records to be meaningful.

Other stories worthy of note: September is the peak of hurricane season. This year, no tropical system affected anyone in the Southeast. For our region, that was a welcome non-event. If we were along the New England coast, the big September story would be the strong early fall Nor'easter that hammered the region for several days. Here, however, we had three cool, breezy days. September showed how different our weather can be from one place to the next. The wet stretch from September 18–24 turned an otherwise dry month into an average or even wetter-than-average one in a narrow band along the Blue Ridge and into southwest Virginia. How'd We Do? Beginning with this month's recap, we'll grade our monthly outlook for temperature and precipitation. Here's how we did… Temperature Forecast Grade: A Our September outlook called for warmer-than-average temperatures. That verified. Every station finished above normal, by an average of about 5 degrees. Precipitation Forecast Grade: B We called for slightly below-average rain. Judged by the national map, that earns a B: the month came in drier than we said. The zoomed-in map makes a case for an A. It shows a band near or above normal, and we leaned toward a less-dry month three weeks before that wet stretch arrived. We wouldn't change a thing in that forecast. Still, we'll grade by what our stations actually collected, about 70 percent of normal. That's drier than we forecast, so we'll take the B. The Typical October: The Turn to Fall "Then summer fades and passes and October comes. We'll smell smoke then, and feel an unexpected sharpness, a thrill of nervousness, swift elation, a sense of sadness and departure."— Asheville’s Thomas Wolfe, in “You Can’t Go Home Again” October is the month the season turns. Average highs fall almost ten degrees from September, and average lows fall more than that. The first frost arrives in the mountain region (and maybe the Foothills) most years, and a touch of snow is possible by the end of the month for elevations above 2500’. The chill, the unease (or thrill for some) of colder weather, and the truth that our summer is over—Wolfe captured all that. October is also one of the driest months of the year. Summer thunderstorms are difficult to generate. Rain comes from fronts and from what the tropics send our way. The leaves turn from the high peaks in early October to the Foothills by month’s end.

The Big Picture The cover image for this document shows the ECMWF forecast for precipitation and temperature anomalies in October. We agree with its temperature guidance but favor a slightly wetter month, for reasons given below. The first few days of October will be the warmest of the month by a wide margin. High pressure will hold over the East while the remnants of a Pacific hurricane lift Gulf moisture into the region. The result is a warm, humid, wet start. The heaviest rain will fall over the southern mountains. The High Country, the Foothills and southwest Virginia will get less. A Canadian front will drive through by October 5th, ending the warm spell and bringing drier weather. Cold air will bank against the east side of the Blue Ridge. The Foothills will run cooler than the mountains for a few days under the clouds. The fly in the ointment is a large area of rain to our south. One model brings it north into the region. It is worth watching. The second half of the month is less certain. The models disagree more than usual on where the ridge sits, but none of them shows a major cold outbreak. Temperatures will run near average. With the season falling fast, near average will feel like fall. Rain will run below average in the third week and slightly below in the fourth. Three things concern us about the rain forecast. First, one good rain event can wipe out three dry weeks, as it did in September. Second, El Niño’s moisture from the south becomes more of a factor as October ends. Third, while an Atlantic tropical system is unlikely to reach us, another Pacific storm remnant could, as Hurricane Polo will in the first week. None of these is in the forecast, but all are on the table as a record-breaking El Niño develops. That looming challenge in the Pacific curbed our enthusiasm for a drier or warmer forecast. For reference, the NOAA October forecast as of the date of this publication is similar on temperatures but slightly wetter than our forecast. The Ocean: El Niño Stays on Track El Niño keeps strengthening on schedule. Sea surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region now run more than 2°C above average. The Climate Prediction Center gives better than a 90% chance of a very strong event this fall and winter. There is a strong possibility it will pass 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 as the strongest El Niño on record. No event since records began in 1950 has held the level now forecast for this winter. As a change of pace this month, here is an animation of El Niño’s development over the last four to five weeks. This one has the classic shape. The warmest water sits in the eastern Pacific off South America, not near the Date Line. Buckle up for an El Niño winter in the Southeast: a very active southern jet stream, more storms, and cooler, wetter weather than average. October is early for those effects. Strong El Niño Octobers tend to run warm across the country, with the wet weather held to the Gulf Coast. The Southeast’s turn to a wet pattern usually comes in late October or November. The real impact arrives in winter. We will publish our 2026-27 Fearless Winter Forecast in the third week of October. Sep 30, 2026 See all Golf-O-Meter 0 Golfballs Only ducks or polar bears. Good day for knitting. Maybe, if you are brave. Worth taking a chance. A good day to be outside. Bosses, you'd better stand at the door. (Or will bosses be first out the door?) ; The Big Picture; The cover image for this document shows the ECMWF forecast for precipitation and temperature anomalies in October. We agree with its temperature guidance but favor a slightly wetter month, for reasons given below.; The first few days of October will be the warmest of the month by a wide margin. High pressure will hold over the East while the remnants of a Pacific hurricane lift Gulf moisture into the region. The result is a warm, humid, wet start. The heaviest rain will fall over the southern mountains. The High Country, the Foothills and southwest Virginia will get less.; A Canadian front will drive through by October 5th, ending the warm spell and bringing drier weather. Cold air will bank against the east side of the Blue Ridge. The Foothills will run cooler than the mountains for a few days under the clouds. The fly in the ointment is a large area of rain to our south. One model brings it north into the region. It is worth watching.; The second half of the month is less certain. The models disagree more than usual on where the ridge sits, but none of them shows a major cold outbreak. Temperatures will run near average. With the season falling fast, near average will feel like fall. Rain will run below average in the third week and slightly below in the fourth.; Three things concern us about the rain forecast. First, one good rain event can wipe out three dry weeks, as it did in September. Second, El Niño’s moisture from the south becomes more of a factor as October ends. Third, while an Atlantic tropical system is unlikely to reach us, another Pacific storm remnant could, as Hurricane Polo will in the first week. None of these is in the forecast, but all are on the table as a record-breaking El Niño develops. That looming challenge in the Pacific curbed our enthusiasm for a drier or warmer forecast.; For reference, the NOAA October forecast as of the date of this publication is similar on temperatures but slightly wetter than our forecast.; The Ocean: El Niño Stays on Track; El Niño keeps strengthening on schedule. Sea surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region now run more than 2°C above average. The Climate Prediction Center gives better than a 90% chance of a very strong event this fall and winter. There is a strong possibility it will pass 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 as the strongest El Niño on record. No event since records began in 1950 has held the level now forecast for this winter.; As a change of pace this month, here is an animation of El Niño’s development over the last four to five weeks.; This one has the classic shape. The warmest water sits in the eastern Pacific off South America, not near the Date Line. Buckle up for an El Niño winter in the Southeast: a very active southern jet stream, more storms, and cooler, wetter weather than average.; October is early for those effects. Strong El Niño Octobers tend to run warm across the country, with the wet weather held to the Gulf Coast. The Southeast’s turn to a wet pattern usually comes in late October or November. The real impact arrives in winter.
